citation: docs/architecture.md, agent state and seen-ness; MIP-3 section 8, which gives the daemon the finish and the window the look
why:
`done` is the state attention routing is built on, and it is the only one of the five no daemon can decide alone: it is an agent that finished while nobody looked. muster-daemon knows when an agent finished and holds it on the pane's record as `finished_unseen`; only a window knows whether somebody was looking, because only the shell sees its own focus. So a window paints a pane carrying the fact as `done`, and a window that shows it while it has the keyboard reports it seen, which clears it for every window.

These cases are the window's half. Each event is a pane's record as its daemon now has it, and `reported` is every pane the window told its daemon it had seen, in order. They are worth pinning as data rather than as tests because the rule is small, entirely about edges, and every edge is a way for the product's whole reason to exist to be quietly wrong: a `done` that never appears routes nobody, and a `done` that appears for a pane somebody watched finish trains the user to ignore it.

The events are a sequence on purpose. Whether a finish was seen depends on what the window was showing when it arrived, so a case that set up state and asked one question would be pinning a snapshot rather than the rule.

cases.name: an agent that finishes in front of you is idle, and its daemon is told
cases.why: The case that keeps `done` meaningful. If finishing on a pane somebody is looking at still raised `done`, every completed agent would raise it and the state would carry no information at all. The daemon cannot see the window, so it records the finish anyway, and the report is what clears it for every other window.

cases.name: an agent that finishes while the window is unfocused is done
cases.why: The pane is on screen, so every input a daemon could have says somebody saw it. Only the window knows nobody was there.

cases.name: an agent that finishes on a pane no window shows is done
cases.why: The other half of unseen, and the one that makes a roster worth having: a focused window says nothing about a pane it is not showing. Attention routing exists to surface these, so reading them as idle would hide exactly what it is for.

cases.name: looking at a pane that finished unseen settles it
cases.why: `done` is a request for attention, so attention has to be able to answer it. A `done` that survived being looked at would sit there forever and become something the user learns to scroll past.

cases.name: bringing a pane on screen settles what finished while it was hidden
cases.why: The same settling reached the other way. Focus and visibility are two inputs to one question, and a rule that only watched focus would leave a pane surfaced from the sidebar still claiming nobody had seen it.

cases.name: a pane coming on screen in an unfocused window is still unseen
cases.why: Both inputs are required, and this is where a rule that treated either as sufficient would show it. A window rearranging itself in the background - a daemon reconnecting, a tab settling - is not somebody looking.

cases.name: a pane reported seen is idle before its daemon answers
cases.why: The window paints what it just saw rather than waiting a round trip for the daemon to agree, or a pane somebody is looking at would stay `done` under their eyes - for longer on a devenv, and for as long as a daemon that never answers takes.

cases.name: looking away does not un-see what you already saw
cases.why: Once the daemon has cleared the finish there is nothing left to un-see. If losing focus could resurrect `done`, every pane in the window would raise one the moment the user switched to a browser, which is the notification behaviour people disable products over.

cases.name: a finish another window saw is idle here too
cases.why: The reason the fact lives in the daemon. Two windows each keeping their own idea of what had been seen left one of them saying `done` about a pane somebody had already read in the other.

cases.name: an agent that goes back to work is working, not done
cases.why: Anything busy means the agent is doing something, so the pane is no longer waiting on anybody, and the daemon clears the finish as it says so. A pane that kept its `done` while visibly working would be showing two states at once.

cases.name: an agent that finishes unseen and then asks for a person is blocked
cases.why: Blocked is the state attention routing exists for, and it must not be masked by a stale `done` from the completion before it. Both are requests for a person; the newer one says what is actually wanted.

cases.name: an agent that ends while working is done
cases.why: A crash, or a one-shot run reaching its end, leaves no agent in the pane to be idle. The daemon counts it as a finish, and somebody who left an agent working wants to hear that it stopped however it stopped.

cases.name: an idle the daemon says finished nothing is idle
cases.why: Only the daemon's finish makes a `done`. A pane whose harness could not be classified and then read as idle never finished anything, and announcing work that was never done is worse than the `unknown` it came from, because it is confident.

cases.name: two daemons that hand out the same pane id are two panes
cases.why: Every daemon names its first pane `w1:p1`. A set keyed by pane alone would let the devenv's agent finishing unseen mark the laptop's pane as waiting, and would tell the laptop's daemon about a look at the devenv - and the user would be sent to the wrong machine, which is the failure attention routing is least able to afford.

cases.name: a pane that finished before the window opened is done
cases.why: A daemon outlives the app, so quitting and coming back is the ordinary case, and agents finish in between. The window saw none of it; the daemon kept the finish for exactly this.

cases.name: a pane that finished before the window opened is reported once it is looked at
cases.why: Arriving is not looking. The window reports it when it first has the keyboard with the pane on screen, the same as a finish it watched arrive.

cases.name: a pane that finished before the window opened, arriving in front of you, is reported
cases.why: A window coming up in front of somebody shows the panes it arrives with, and a finish on one of them is seen the moment it is drawn.

cases.name: a pane the daemon says nobody needs is not made into a request
cases.why: Adopting the daemon's answer means adopting it when it says idle too - inventing a `done` for a pane it never raised one for would fill a fresh window with requests nobody made, which costs the state its meaning just as surely as never raising it.

cases.name: a window that has never been told about focus has seen nothing
cases.why: The starting state, and it is deliberately the pessimistic one. A core that assumed it was focused until told otherwise would report every agent seen during startup - the window is not on screen yet, and startup is exactly when a session full of running agents is being read for the first time.

cases.name: a pane that closes takes what was held about it, so the next pane to be called that is new
cases.why: Ids belong to the daemon and it reuses them - a restarted daemon brings each pane back under its old name - so nothing held about a pane can outlive it. Left behind, a report still waiting for its answer is inherited: the next pane with that id finishes in front of somebody, the window believes it already said so, and every other window goes on showing it `done`.

cases.name: a daemon that comes back is told again what is on screen
cases.why: A report sent as the connection dropped may never have arrived, and the daemon would go on saying `done` to every other window. What the window is showing when the connection returns is reported again; a daemon that did hear the first one answers that it already knew.

cases.name: a daemon that comes back has its finishes off screen shown as done again
cases.why: What the daemon still holds may be a finish it never heard was seen, or a new one that arrived while the connection was down, and the window cannot tell which. `done` is the answer that can be wrong only by asking somebody to look.

cases.name: a daemon coming back takes back only its own reports
cases.why: The devenv's connection dropping says nothing about what the laptop's daemon heard.

cases.name: a report the daemon refused is done again
cases.why: A daemon handing its panes to another refuses every change, `Seen` included, and a handoff that then fails keeps the connection, so nothing reports the pane again. The daemon and every other window still say `done`; painting it `idle` here would be this window alone claiming the finish was seen.

cases.name: a pane whose report was refused is reported at the next look
cases.why: Not at once: a daemon still refusing would refuse again, as fast as it could answer. The next time somebody looks is the next report, and a daemon that is serving again takes it.

cases.name: an agent waiting on its own work is not laid over with done
cases.why: The daemon sets no finish while an agent waits and clears one when it declares a wait, so the two should never meet. If a finish this window holds meets a wait anyway, the wait wins: the agent said it has not finished, and calling it done would send somebody to a pane with nothing for them.
